headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: ms-swift can write and egress while caveman uses MCP and shared files, creating unsafe pairwise workflows.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: caveman uses MCP and reads/writes project files like CLAUDE.md, while ms-swift can read/write files and run CLI/Python workflows. That creates a plausible path where content from ms-swift outputs is copied into caveman’s trusted files or MCP-fed context. No direct shared channel is documented, so uncertainty keeps this at medium rather than high.
conditions: IF ms-swift output is pasted into CLAUDE.md or another caveman-trusted file
IF caveman ingests ms-swift-generated text through MCP or file reads without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable MCP for caveman during cross-agent workflows
Keep ms-swift outputs in a separate scratch directory
Add a manual review step before caveman consumes any ms-swift text
Prefix imported text with provenance markers
requires-engineering: add content provenance filtering between the agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Both agents touch files, and ms-swift explicitly handles hub_token and sdk-token while also allowing network egress. caveman touches session logs, memory files, and project notes. If they share a workspace, sensitive material can flow from caveman into ms-swift and then out over allowlisted network paths. The shared-workspace assumption is not explicit, so this is medium, not high.
conditions: IF caveman and ms-swift share a filesystem or workspace
IF ms-swift is run on files containing session logs, memory files, project notes, or tokens
mitigations: Separate the agents into different directories
Remove secrets from any shared workspace before running ms-swift
Restrict ms-swift network egress to a test endpoint
Review logs for accidental secret inclusion
requires-engineering: enforce workspace isolation and secret redaction

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ms-swift can write the filesystem, execute shells, and spawn subprocesses; caveman supports multiple instances and uses files plus MCP. Even though caveman’s own write capability is not stated, the pair can still contend over shared mutable files or generated artifacts. Because shared-state behavior is not stated, the conflict is plausible but not proven, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF both agents operate in the same directory tree
IF caveman and ms-swift modify overlapping files or generated outputs
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory
Serialize writes with a simple operator-managed lock file
Avoid concurrent runs on the same repo
Check for file diffs before merging outputs
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: caveman is a content-writing agent that can consume files and MCP-fed context, while ms-swift can generate training, evaluation, or configuration outputs. If caveman treats ms-swift output as authoritative, errors can cascade into polished but wrong content. No verification mechanism is documented, so the interaction exists in default workflows but is not guaranteed.
conditions: IF caveman uses ms-swift-generated text as source material
IF no human or automated verification step checks ms-swift outputs before caveman rewrites them
mitigations: Require a second-pass human review
Compare ms-swift outputs against source data before reuse
Mark generated text as untrusted in the workflow
Limit caveman to editing only verified inputs
requires-engineering: add automated validation gates

E_compliance.rationale: ms-swift explicitly handles hub_token and sdk-token and can write logs, checkpoints, and configuration files; caveman touches session logs and memory files. That combination raises retention and secret-handling concerns if the pair is used on regulated or credentialed data. The profiles do not state residency or certifications, so I cannot escalate beyond medium.
conditions: IF regulated data or credentials are stored in the shared workspace
IF logs, checkpoints, or memory files are retained beyond the operator's policy
mitigations: Purge logs after each run
Keep credentials out of shared directories
Use a dedicated retention policy for checkpoints and notes
Review whether any regulated data is present before execution
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls
